name: Matsutake (pine mushroom) - Iwate and Nagano production
text: Japanese matsutake are harvested across Honshu, but Iwate and Nagano compete for first and second place in annual output. Harvest moves north to south: Tohoku (Iwate etc.) roughly mid-September to mid-October, Chubu (Nagano etc.) late September to mid-October, Kinki (Hyogo etc.) early to late October. Output has been described as declining year on year.
flavor: Sellers describe Iwate matsutake as balanced in aroma, texture and umami, and Nagano matsutake as strongly aromatic with a crisp bite; these are trade descriptions, not measured grades.
use: Grilled, in dobin-mushi and matsutake gohan; sold fresh in season at prices that move sharply with origin and cap opening.
craft: Yield depends on weather: a rainy, cool late August to mid-September favours a good year, while a hot, dry spell tends to give a poor one, so expect price swings. Sellers attribute Nagano's aroma to high-altitude mountains with large day-night temperature swings (a sales claim). Check stalk thickness and springiness and clean, undamaged gills.
src: Dash - domestic matsutake season by region

name: Matsutake growth-stage names (koro, tsubomi, chu-tsubomi, hiraki)
ja: 松茸の発育段階(ころ・つぼみ・中つぼみ・開き)
text: There is no nationwide shipping standard for matsutake. Instead the trade names the mushroom by development stage: koro, tsubomi, chu-tsubomi (middle bud) and hiraki (open). Price depends heavily on shipping date and on how far the cap has opened.
flavor: Closed-cap stages are the premium end of the market; open caps sell for less.
use: Used as the working vocabulary when ordering or quoting matsutake; the stage decides price and the dish it is bought for.
craft: Because no official grade table exists, specify stage, size and origin in the order rather than a grade. Selection cues in the sources: thick, springy stalk and gills free of dirt. Sources are mostly dealers and blogs, so treat the stage-to-price relationship as trade practice.
src: Dash - domestic matsutake season and types

name: Donko (thick-capped dried shiitake, 冬菇)
text: Donko is the dried shiitake class whose cap has opened less than about 7 tenths (7-bu), leaving a hemispherical, thick-fleshed cap. It is sorted by cap size; one Oita wholesaler handles donko in four size grades. Retail labels give about 5-6 cm for donko, 3-4 cm for small donko and 6-7 cm for large donko, but these are shop labels, not a common standard.
flavor: Dense, meaty cap with concentrated flavour once rehydrated.
use: Simmered whole (nimono, chikuzen-ni), where the thick cap holds shape and gives chew.
craft: Judge by cap closure, thickness and size grade. The sources give only qualitative thickness terms (thick vs thin), with no millimetre standard found. Confirm the supplier's own size grade rather than relying on the word donko alone.
src: Himeno Ichiro Shoten - shiitake types and quality

name: Koshin (open-capped dried shiitake, 香信)
text: Koshin is dried shiitake whose cap has opened about 7 tenths or more, giving a flat, thin-fleshed cap. One Oita wholesaler grades koshin into four size classes. Caps are also sorted by diameter into large-, medium- and small-leaf (dai-ba, chu-ba, sho-ba) classes.
flavor: Lighter, more delicate body than donko; thinner flesh rehydrates quickly.
use: Sliced or chopped for chirashi, soups, stir-cooked dishes, makizushi filling and dashi where speed and even cooking matter more than meatiness.
craft: Check flatness and cap diameter class. As with donko, the sources give no millimetre thickness standard, so specify size class with the supplier.
src: Himeno Ichiro Shoten - shiitake types and quality

name: Koko (half-open dried shiitake, 香菇)
text: Koko is the intermediate dried shiitake class, with the cap opened to about 5 tenths, between donko and koshin. One Oita wholesaler sorts koko into three size grades, against four for donko and four for koshin.
flavor: Between the meatiness of donko and the thin lightness of koshin.
use: General-purpose dried shiitake for simmered dishes and rice dishes when donko is too costly and koshin too thin.
craft: Class is set by degree of cap opening, then size. The cap-opening fractions come from trade explanations rather than a legal standard.
src: Himeno Ichiro Shoten - shiitake types and quality

name: Oita log-grown dried shiitake
text: Oita, Miyazaki and Kumamoto together produce about 70 percent of Japan's dried shiitake, according to one trade source. The Oita Prefecture Shiitake Agricultural Cooperative sells donko, koshin and small-cap donko lines. The sources do not give a standardized thickness grade.
flavor: Log-grown dried shiitake are sold on aroma and flesh thickness.
use: Dashi, simmered dishes and rice dishes; the cap class decides the use.
craft: Specify cap class (donko, koko, koshin), size grade and origin when buying. The percentage share is from a single trade source and should be checked against official statistics.
src: Himeno Ichiro Shoten - shiitake types and quality

name: Warabi and zenmai (bracken and flowering fern shoots)
text: Both ferns must be de-bittered before eating; raw they can cause food poisoning. Season is given as April-May by some sources and mid-March to early June by others; the Akita prefectural page gives May to August for warabi, so timing depends on altitude and climate.
flavor: Slippery, mild, slightly sweet after aku removal.
use: Ohitashi, nimono, soups, and dried forms preserved for later use.
craft: Aku is stronger the longer after picking, so treat promptly. Pour boiling water over the shoots with baking soda and leave overnight; wood ash is the traditional alternative. Do not eat untreated.

name: Kogomi (ostrich fern fiddleheads)
text: Kogomi is a low-aku sansai. The Akita prefectural page gives late April to late May, while another source says March to mid-June, so timing varies by region.
flavor: Mild, clean, little bitterness.
use: Ohitashi, tempura and goma-ae.
craft: Cut off the hard base and soak about 10 minutes in water; little aku means it needs less treatment than warabi or zenmai.

name: Fukinoto (butterbur flower buds)
text: Fukinoto is among the first spring sansai. Many sources say February-April; the Akita page gives early March to early May. Kanto lowlands can see it in early March while Tohoku mountains only in late April.
flavor: Bitter, aromatic, an early-spring bite.
use: Fukinoto-miso, tempura, soup garnish.
craft: Split by hand and soak about 10 minutes before use. A safety point: fukinoto is easily mistaken for the poisonous hashiridokoro (Scopolia), so identify the plant reliably when sourcing wild.

name: Taranome and udo (spring sansai shoots)
text: Wild taranome is given as April to early June and udo as March to May, depending on region and elevation. Both are prepared quickly after harvest.
flavor: Taranome is slightly bitter and rich; udo is crisp and aromatic.
use: Taranome in tempura; udo raw in salads and vinegar dishes, or simmered.
craft: Taranome: remove the hard base and the scales (hakama), then soak in water to remove aku. Udo: cut surfaces discolour quickly, so work promptly and acidulate or soak. Seasons vary widely by locality.

name: Tanba kuro-daizu (Tanba black soybean)
text: Named 'Tanba-guro' in 1941 by the Hyogo agricultural experiment station from a landrace grown in the Tanba area; the Taki-gun-shi (1918) gives origin as Kawakita, Saiki-cho, now Tanba-Sasayama. Hundred-grain weight is 80-90 g versus about 30 g for ordinary black soybeans. It takes about 1.5 times the roughly 70-day flowering-to-maturity period of normal soybeans. Thick skin resists disintegration. Main area is Hyogo (Tanba-Sasayama, Tanba, Tajima, Nishi- and Higashi-Harima); also Okayama and Shiga.
flavor: Very large, plump beans that stay intact when simmered.
use: Kuro-mame for osechi, simmered whole.
craft: Harvest timing sources differ: one dealer says mid-November, JA Tajima gives early to mid December as peak in Asago. Buy by lot and harvest year; skin integrity and size matter for kuro-mame.

name: Tanba dainagon azuki
text: A large-grained, barrel-shaped azuki that JA Zennoh Hyogo says is suited to yude-azuki and tsubuan, with few split skins, belly cracks or disintegration on cooking. Grown in Tanba, Tanba-Sasayama, Kanzaki-gun and Tajima.
flavor: Large, plump, intact cooked beans.
use: Boiled sweet azuki, tsubuan, and confections where whole beans matter.
craft: Low skin splitting and belly cracking make it good for whole-bean sweets. No harvest-date or grade data came up in the searches.
src: Tanba no Kurotaro - raw Tanba beans

name: Nagaimo (Chinese yam)
text: Cylindrical yam with high water content and relatively mild stickiness and a light taste. Aomori and Hokkaido together account for more than 70 percent of the market for yamaimo, followed by Nagano, Gunma and Chiba. Yams store well and are sold year-round, partly from spring digging after overwintering in the soil.
flavor: Watery, crisp when raw, light and clean.
use: Cut raw (sengiri, sticks), grated for light tororo, grilled.
craft: Less sticky than yamato-imo or jinenjo, so use it where body or crispness matters rather than binding. The market-share figure covers yamaimo overall.

name: Ichoimo and tsukune-imo (the two 'yamato-imo')
ja: いちょう芋・つくね芋(大和芋)
text: Ichoimo is flat, fan-shaped; tsukune-imo is round. In Kanto ichoimo is called yamato-imo, in Kansai tsukune-imo carries that name. Both are stickier than nagaimo. Tsukune-imo is grown mainly in Nara, Mie, Wakayama and Ehime. Peak harvest is described as around the first frosts, when stickiness and sweetness are strongest.
flavor: Dense, very sticky, richer than nagaimo.
use: Tororo, binder for soba and kamaboko-type dishes, grated toppings.
craft: Confirm which yam a supplier means by 'yamato-imo' because the name differs between Kanto and Kansai. Ichoimo and tsukune stickiness is ranked behind only jinenjo.

name: Kaga maruimo, Ise-imo and Tanba-imo (regional yamato-imo)
ja: 加賀まるいも・伊勢いも・丹波いも
text: Sources list these as regional specialities of the yamato-imo type: Kaga maruimo (Ishikawa), Ise-imo (Mie and Nara) and Tanba-imo (Hyogo).
flavor: Sticky, dense yams of the yamato-imo type.
use: Tororo, steamed and grated dishes, binder.
craft: The sources give only the region listing, with no cultivar, harvest or grade data.

name: Naruto Kintoki sweet potato
text: A sweet potato from Naruto, Tokushima, grown mainly in coastal sandy fields of north-east Tokushima such as Naruto and Matsushige. It has chestnut-like, fluffy flesh and refined sweetness and keeps well. It belongs to the Koukei 14 line, as do Goroshima Kintoki and Sakaide Kintoki.
flavor: Chestnut-like, dry and floury, gently sweet.
use: Roasted, steamed, tempura and sweets.
craft: Storage extends sweetness: do not wash, dry in a ventilated place 2-3 days before storing. Sources differ on storage length.

name: Goroshima Kintoki sweet potato
text: Sweet potato grown in the Goroshima district of Kanazawa, Ishikawa, in the Koukei 14 line like Naruto Kintoki and Sakaide Kintoki (Kagawa). Output is small and the name is a registered trademark, so only designated growers may ship under it.
flavor: Floury, sweeter after storage.
use: Roasted, steamed and sweets.
craft: Sweetness is said to rise with storage into winter. Verify trademark origin when it is specified on the menu.

name: Konnyaku-imo of Gunma (konjac corm)
text: Gunma is first in the country with a 90-plus percent share: 50,200 t and 93.5 percent in 2020, 49,200 t and 94.8 percent in 2022. Cultivars include Haruna-kuro, Akagi-odama, Konnyaku Norin 3 and Miyamamasari. Akagi-odama has rod-shaped seed corms (kiko), disease resistance and high yield. Sources disagree on shares: Numata gives Akagi-odama 64 percent and Miyamamasari 28 percent of output, Kan-etsu about 80 percent Akagi-odama, while another says Miyamamasari is the most planted.
flavor: Raw corm is not eaten; quality shows in the finished konnyaku.
use: Raw material for konnyaku and shirataki.
craft: Cultivar shares differ by source and by area vs production measure, so check the year and basis.

name: Fukuchi White Roppen garlic (Aomori)
text: Aomori produces about 70 percent of domestic garlic shipments. The cultivar originates in the Fukuchi district of Nanbu-cho (former Fukuchi-mura) and spread in neighbouring Takko, known as the garlic town. Large white cloves, firm flesh, high sugar, four to six cloves per bulb. Harvest is late June to early July.
flavor: Large, white, firm cloves with sweetness.
use: Raw grated, grilled, and as seasoning garlic.
craft: After harvest, dry about one month, then store and ship year-round. Late-maturing type.

name: Awaji onion (Awaji-shima tamanegi)
text: Awaji harvests by maturity group. A Minamiawaji-cited summary gives gokuwase early March, wase early April, chusei mid-May, chubansei late May onward. Another source gives late-maturing harvest early-mid June, with Momiji no Kagayaki among the cultivars. Mid- and late types are dried in huts before shipping. A late type can keep about a year, according to a retailer.
flavor: Sweet and soft; sugar rises with storage per one seller.
use: Raw sliced, onion gratin, simmered.
craft: Shin-tamanegi is a harvest-timing term, not a cultivar, and keeps poorly. Sources differ on figures, so confirm with Minamiawaji City or Hyogo.

name: Buna-shimeji (Nagano bed-grown)
text: Nagano is the birthplace of artificial buna-shimeji cultivation and first nationally: 47,428.6 t, 40.5 percent in the Reiwa 6 forest-products statistics. Production is in bottles/beds on sawdust, mainly cedar aged over six months. Inoculation to harvest takes about 120 days per an older source. Main areas are Hokushin and Nagano.
flavor: Mild, firm texture.
use: Sauteed, simmered, in soups and takikomi.
craft: The 120-day figure is from a roughly 20-year-old article. Sawdust aging removes aku.

name: Maitake (Niigata bed-grown)
text: Niigata is first: 35,642.2 t in 2023, 67.1 percent share in 2020. Niigata, Shizuoka and Fukuoka make up about 84 percent. Nagano is fourth, 2,763 t in 2020 and 2,615 t in 2023.
flavor: Aromatic, chewy; the sources do not detail flavour.
use: Tempura, soup, sauteed, takikomi.
craft: The sources give production statistics only, with no cultivation or grading detail.
